kaigo-skills-mock-01.title: Care Skills Evaluation Test — Practice Form 01

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q01.prompt: Which support respects the person’s choices in daily life?
options: Make choices for them based on staff experience.
Ask about the person’s wishes and help with the parts that need support.
Check family opinions and tell the person the result.
Withhold necessary assistance if the person can choose.
rationales: Staff experience is useful but does not justify unilaterally taking over choices the person can make.
Starting with the person’s wishes and helping with the parts needed to put them into practice respects self-determination.
Family-only decisions followed by notification omit the person’s opportunity to choose.
Choosing independently differs from needing assistance to act. Do not withhold necessary help.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q02.prompt: Which directly indicates the person’s experienced quality of life?
options: Their satisfaction and sense of purpose.
The facility’s average room area.
The number of staff tasks completed daily.
The number of seats prepared for weekly events.
rationales: Satisfaction and purpose directly describe subjective quality of life.
Average room area describes the environment, not personal satisfaction directly.
Staff task counts describe workload, not feelings about daily life.
Seat counts describe preparation, not confirmed enjoyment or satisfaction.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q03.prompt: What is evaluation after support following a care plan?
options: Gather information and organize daily-life issues.
Write support goals and content into the plan.
Provide support following the plan.
Check goal achievement and whether the plan fits.
rationales: Gathering information and organizing issues mainly belongs to assessment.
Writing goals and support is planning, distinct from evaluation after implementation.
Following the plan is implementation, distinct from evaluating results.
Evaluation compares outcomes with goals and checks whether the plan suited the person.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q04.prompt: How should information learned in the person’s room be handled?
options: Explain details in a shop to anyone at the same workplace.
Send family-requested records to private contacts.
Share with necessary recipients according to consent and procedures.
Post updates on personal social media with names omitted.
rationales: Even coworkers can expose personal information to bystanders by discussing details in a shop.
Do not send records to a private contact solely at the family’s request. Check the person’s consent and the facility’s procedures.
This checks why sharing is needed, who needs the information, the person’s consent and the applicable procedures.
Omitting names may still allow identification. Avoid personal social-media posts.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q05.prompt: After toileting care, you remove used gloves. What comes next?
options: Continue with the next care task if the hands look clean.
Disinfect only the surface of new gloves.
Wash the hands after the next care task is finished.
Perform hand hygiene after removing gloves.
rationales: A clean appearance does not establish absence of contamination. Hand hygiene cannot be omitted.
Disinfecting new gloves does not replace hand hygiene after glove removal.
Waiting until after the next care task may spread contamination in the meantime.
Hands can still be contaminated after removal, so perform appropriate hand hygiene.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q06.prompt: Which action may restrict the person’s movement?
options: Listen in a quiet place they requested.
Lock the room so they cannot leave.
Walk together at their pace in the corridor.
Check their walking aid before departure.
rationales: Listening in the requested place does not restrict movement as described.
Locking them in restricts freedom of movement.
Matching walking pace differs from unilaterally restricting movement.
Checking equipment supports safe mobility; the description does not confine the person.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q07.prompt: Which is an example of psychological abuse?
options: Hit an arm hard and cause injury.
Use savings for personal shopping without permission.
Repeatedly threaten with frightening words.
Leave someone without needed meal assistance for a long time.
rationales: Hitting hard and causing injury is physical abuse.
Unauthorized personal use of savings is financial abuse.
Repeated threatening words causing fear are psychological abuse.
Withholding necessary meal support and leaving the person is neglect.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q08.prompt: Which cooperation between care workers and other professions is appropriate?
options: Report observed changes and consult about necessary judgments.
Change medication amounts, then tell healthcare professionals the result.
Omit observation times while waiting for healthcare professionals to check.
Omit wishes because professionals will handle support.
rationales: This communicates changes confirmed in daily contact and seeks professional judgment.
Care workers must not independently change medication amounts before notification.
Observation times help interpret changes and must not be omitted while awaiting consultation.
The person’s wishes also inform support. Do not leave them out because a professional will take over.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q09.prompt: You find damage to a planned walking aid. What is appropriate?
options: Use it briefly because it is familiar.
Do not start use; report damage to the person responsible.
Try it while searching for the same model.
Switch to a similar aid and check after use.
rationales: Even short-distance use is not established as safe with damaged equipment.
Do not begin using the damaged aid. Report the damage and check a safe method or alternative.
Do not try damaged equipment on the person even while seeking a replacement.
Similar aids may fit differently. Check before, not after, use.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q10.prompt: Which reporting approach is appropriate after discovering an accident?
options: Promptly report confirmed facts separately from unknowns.
Make first contact only after finishing the written report.
Wait for a confirmed cause before telling those involved.
Save details to report at the next meeting.
rationales: Separating facts and unknowns enables prompt action without waiting for cause confirmation.
Do not delay initial contact to complete paperwork.
Report the discovered accident promptly even if its cause is unknown.
Waiting for the next meeting may delay necessary responses.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q11.prompt: Which understanding of stressors is appropriate?
options: Noise, fatigue and relationships may contribute.
No reported anxiety means no stress.
The same stimulus causes equal stress for everyone.
Enough rest eliminates relationship effects.
rationales: Environmental, physical and interpersonal factors can all contribute to stress.
Not expressing anxiety does not establish absence of stress.
Responses and conditions differ even with identical stimuli.
Rest matters but does not necessarily remove interpersonal effects.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q12.prompt: Which memory function means remembering by recall?
options: Learning new information for the first time.
Continuing to retain learned information.
Directing attention to current stimuli.
Retrieving retained information when needed.
rationales: New learning is encoding, distinct from recalling retained content.
Keeping information is retention, distinct from retrieval.
Attention to stimuli differs from recall of learned content.
Recall retrieves retained information and corresponds to remembering.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q13.prompt: Which approach to age-related changes is appropriate?
options: Use another same-age person’s method without checking.
Avoid reporting new complaints because they are age-related.
Consider life history, current condition and individual differences.
Prioritize life history and omit current responses.
rationales: Same-age people differ in functions and habits. Do not apply one method unchecked.
Do not dismiss new complaints as simply due to age. Check them as a change in condition and communicate what was found.
This combines history and current condition to understand individual support needs.
Current responses as well as history inform support and should be recorded.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q14.prompt: What becomes difficult with disorientation in dementia?
options: Hearing and learning new information.
Organizing a task sequence.
Counting coins and calculating payment.
Recognizing the current date, time or place.
rationales: Difficulty learning new information concerns memory.
Sequence organization relates to executive functions, not date/place recognition.
Calculation and payment difficulties are not orientation itself as asked here.
Orientation recognizes current date, time, place and related context.

options: Bladder.
Kidney.
Esophagus.
Large intestine.
rationales: The bladder temporarily stores urine until urination.
Kidneys produce urine; their role differs from the storage sac.
The esophagus carries food to the stomach and does not store urine.
The large intestine absorbs water and forms stool, among other functions, but does not store urine.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q16.prompt: Which organ contributes to sweating and protection of the body surface?
options: Skin.
Kidney.
Bladder.
Esophagus.
rationales: Skin protects the body surface and produces sweat, among other functions.
Kidneys form urine from waste and other substances in blood; they do not cover the body surface.
The bladder stores urine rather than providing sweating or surface protection.
The esophagus carries food and does not produce sweat.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q17.prompt: Which question lets the person express wishes freely?
options: Will you join today’s activity?
What would you like to try in today’s activity?
Would morning or afternoon be better?
Would you like blue or red materials?
rationales: Asking whether they will join is mainly a closed yes/no question.
This does not restrict desired actions and makes it easier to express wishes in their own words.
Two choices of morning or afternoon restrict answers rather than inviting free expression.
Restricting answers to two colors does not invite an open response.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q18.prompt: The person expresses anxiety. What is appropriate?
options: Listen without interrupting and check what worries them.
Recommend a diversion and change the subject.
Explain the schedule again and ask feelings later.
Say others are attending and record reassurance.
rationales: Listening first and checking the concern acknowledges their experience.
Immediately switching to diversion prevents fully hearing the concern.
Prioritizing the schedule alone leaves the actual worry unconfirmed.
Other people attending does not establish reassurance. Do not record it without checking responses.

options: Convey feelings through expression or gesture.
Indicate a desired destination in writing.
Convey today’s schedule in sign language.
Explain the start time in words.
rationales: Expressions and gestures convey feelings without words.
Writing represents content through language, distinct from nonverbal information here.
Sign language is language. Lack of voice alone does not make it nonverbal.
Explaining time in words conveys verbal information.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q20.prompt: The person says ‘I don’t want to join today,’ but actual participation has not been observed. Which record is appropriate?
options: The person did not attend and stayed in their room.
They wanted to attend, but staff canceled it.
Attendance confirmed; the person wanted rest afterward.
Stated ‘I don’t want to join today.’ Actual participation remains unconfirmed.
rationales: Nonattendance and time in the room have not been observed.
This reverses wishes and adds an unconfirmed staff cancellation.
Neither attendance nor rest afterward is confirmed in this scene.
This separates the person’s words from unchecked actual participation.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q21.prompt: Which describes the significance of mobility?
options: An identical destination allows less explanation.
Arrival establishes that wishes were fulfilled.
Equipment use replaces condition checks.
It expands daily activities and social participation.
rationales: Even with the same destination, explain this occasion and check wishes.
Arrival alone does not establish satisfaction with purpose or time spent.
Equipment use does not replace checks of condition or necessary help.
Mobility expands daily actions, relationships and participation opportunities.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q22.prompt: Which posture describes sitting on a chair?
options: Side-lying.
Standing.
Sitting.
Supine.
rationales: Side-lying means lying on one side.
Standing is upright on the feet, not seated in a chair.
Sitting on a chair is a seated posture.
Supine means lying on the back and differs from sitting.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q23.prompt: Which relates to physical and mental changes after prolonged inactivity?
options: Contact dermatitis.
Urinary tract infection.
Food allergy.
Disuse syndrome.
rationales: Contact dermatitis is skin inflammation, not the overall decline associated with inactivity.
Urinary tract infection is an infection, not this group of physical and mental changes.
Food allergy is a food-related reaction, not inactivity-related change.
Prolonged inactivity-related decline in functions such as muscle strength relates to disuse syndrome.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q24.prompt: Which action is appropriate before mobility assistance?
options: Use previous consent and explain this occasion afterward.
Check destination seating and assess condition after arrival.
Check condition and support, explain and obtain consent.
Decide the method only among staff because the person is hurried.
rationales: Consent on a previous occasion does not automatically apply now. Explain the current condition and the assistance proposed.
Available seating at the destination is not enough; check the person’s condition before moving.
Check the person’s current condition and the method for this occasion, explain them and obtain consent before providing assistance.
Urgency does not justify staff-only decisions without wishes or safety checks.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q25.prompt: Which describes the significance of meals?
options: The same menu removes any need to ask preferences.
Sufficient intake confirms satisfaction.
Suitable nutrition removes the need to consider surroundings.
They provide nutrition, enjoyment and interaction.
rationales: Preferences differ even with the same menu, so it is important to ask what the person would like.
Enough intake does not establish satisfaction with taste or atmosphere; check separately.
The environment and feelings matter as well as nutrition.
Meals provide nutrients and daily-life opportunities for enjoyment and interaction.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q26.prompt: What is chewing food and mixing it with saliva?
options: Swallowing.
Mastication.
Esophageal peristalsis.
Digestion in the stomach.
rationales: Swallowing differs from the chewing-and-saliva stage.
Mastication chews and mixes food with saliva to prepare it for swallowing.
Esophageal peristalsis moves swallowed material, distinct from chewing in the mouth.
Stomach digestion follows delivery to the stomach rather than chewing in the mouth.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q27.prompt: What should be checked before serving?
options: Whether the meal is for this person and matches texture and allergy requirements.
Whether time and dish count match the schedule.
Whether it resembles yesterday’s meal.
Whether dish colors match those of others in the room.
rationales: Identify the person and match individual texture and allergy conditions before serving.
Time and dish count alone do not establish recipient or individual suitability.
Visual resemblance to yesterday does not establish compliance with current instructions.
Matching dish colors does not verify identity or allergy conditions.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q28.prompt: What is appropriate when the person is chewing?
options: Ask a short question requiring an immediate reply.
Repeat questions to check hearing.
Do not request a reply; wait for a suitable time to speak.
Assume no reply means explanation is complete and move on.
rationales: Demanding an immediate reply while chewing interferes with safe eating.
Even a hearing check should not rush replies during chewing.
This avoids requesting speech during chewing and waits until speaking is possible.
Do not interpret silence as understanding; check again at an appropriate time.

options: Cancel planned observation whenever embarrassment is expressed.
Arrange both needed support and screening from others’ view.
Postpone necessary explanation to finish quickly.
Leave the person visible from the corridor for staff convenience.
rationales: Embarrassment alone does not authorize independently canceling necessary observation.
This combines needed help and observation with privacy screening.
Deferring explanation for speed omits understanding or consent.
Protect the person’s privacy rather than leaving them visible from the corridor solely for staff convenience.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q30.prompt: Which correctly pairs passing urine and stool with their names?
options: Urine: defecation; stool: urination.
Urine: urination; stool: defecation.
Urine: urination; stool: urination.
Urine: defecation; stool: defecation.
rationales: The terms are reversed. Passing urine is urination.
Passing urine is urination and passing stool is defecation.
The first is correct, but passing stool is defecation.
The second is correct, but passing urine is urination.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q31.prompt: Which report of changed stool condition is appropriate?
options: Use yesterday’s record and report today as identical.
Name a causal disease from one change.
Omit complaints and convey assumptions as facts.
Report date/time, observed condition and the person’s own words.
rationales: Yesterday’s observation does not confirm today’s condition.
Do not diagnose a cause from one change. Report facts for assessment.
The person’s own account is also necessary information. Do not present assumptions as facts.
This separates when, what was observed and what the person said.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q32.prompt: Only wet trousers have been confirmed. What is appropriate?
options: Record urinary incontinence because clothes were wet.
Record wetness and the unconfirmed cause separately.
Record spilled water because a cup is nearby.
Record no wetness because no reason was given.
rationales: Wet clothing alone does not establish urinary incontinence; this would confirm an unknown cause.
This distinguishes observed wetness from its unknown cause.
A nearby cup does not establish spilled water.
No explanation does not invalidate observed wetness.

options: It helps regulate temperature and protect skin.
Thick clothes replace room-temperature checks.
Any skin-covering clothes work regardless of size.
Seasonal suitability removes the need to consider activity.
rationales: Clothes regulate temperature and protect skin from external stimuli.
Thick clothing does not replace environmental temperature checks; consider heat, cold and condition too.
Unsuitable size can affect comfort and movement despite skin coverage.
Consider activities and condition as well as season.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q34.prompt: What is appropriate before and after dressing assistance?
options: Record completion when clothes are prepared.
Check changes such as comfort and pain.
Omit checks after dressing if the person chose the clothes.
Omit pain complaints if consent was given.
rationales: Preparation differs from actual completed dressing.
Checking comfort and pain before and after helps establish whether methods and clothes fit.
Personal choice does not remove the need to check condition and feelings after dressing.
Pain complaints remain important despite consent and must not be omitted.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q35.prompt: You find gum bleeding or swelling during oral care. What is appropriate?
options: Decide the cause and explain a disease name.
Report observed bleeding or swelling to healthcare professionals.
Choose and apply oral medicine before reporting.
Record usual condition if the person is unconcerned.
rationales: Care workers do not diagnose a cause from bleeding or swelling alone.
Report where the bleeding or swelling was observed and what it was like to healthcare professionals, so that it can be assessed.
Do not independently select medication; report observations and check.
Lack of personal concern does not turn an observed change into normal condition.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q36.prompt: Which describes bathing and maintaining cleanliness?
options: Cleanliness removes the need to ask feelings.
Following schedule allows fewer condition checks.
They relate to comfort and daily rhythm as well as cleanliness.
One method removes the need to consider habit differences.
rationales: Feelings and wishes matter as well as cleanliness.
Following schedule does not justify reducing that day’s checks.
Bathing and hygiene relate to cleanliness, comfort and daily rhythm.
Even the same method needs checking against individual habits and preferences.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q37.prompt: The person declines whole-body support and wants only a discussion about face washing. What is appropriate?
options: Face-washing wishes mean consent to whole-body support.
Declining whole-body support cancels the face-washing discussion.
Separate face-washing discussion from consent to whole-body support.
Treat receiving the request for discussion as completed face washing.
rationales: A face-washing discussion is not blanket consent to whole-body support.
The face-washing discussion remains wanted despite declining whole-body assistance.
This distinguishes the discussion the person requested from whole-body assistance to which they have not consented.
A discussion request does not establish actual face washing.

options: Shopping for necessary items.
Bringing food to one’s mouth at the table.
Urinating while seated on the toilet.
Putting an arm through a jacket sleeve.
rationales: Shopping is an instrumental activity supporting daily life.
Bringing food to the mouth is a basic daily activity.
Urinating on the toilet is a basic elimination activity.
Putting on clothing is a basic daily activity.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q39.prompt: What is appropriate before organizing possessions?
options: Discard old items and show the remainder afterward.
Let staff decide unwanted items because tidying was requested.
Check retained items and the method with the person and obtain consent.
Follow family sorting preferences and tell the person afterward.
rationales: Discarding first prevents prior personal choice of what to keep.
A tidying request does not authorize staff freely deciding what is unnecessary.
Check with the person which items to keep and how to organize them, and obtain consent to the specific work.
Check the person’s wishes and consent rather than proceeding solely according to the family’s sorting preferences.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q40.prompt: What should be checked before washing clothes?
options: Wash same-color items identically.
Continue the previous owner’s method without checking.
Check the method against material and care labels.
Wash lightly soiled items without reading labels.
rationales: Identical colors can have different materials or instructions and need different washing.
Check this garment’s labels and material before continuing a prior method.
Material and care labels help select suitable handling.
Little dirt does not justify skipping material or label checks.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q41.prompt: What is appropriate before using the illustrated route?
options: Check the box with the responsible person and secure route safety before use.
Proceed beside box B because destination A is correct.
Treat the whole route as checked because you waited at C.
Ask the person to step over B and proceed.
rationales: The box obstructs passage, so check with the responsible person and establish safety first.
The correct destination does not resolve the box hazard.
Waiting at C alone does not establish safety of the whole route.
Secure a safe route rather than asking the person to cross an obstacle.
kaigo-skills-mock-01-q41.figureDescription: The diagram is a top view of a route. A is the destination, B a large box in the route, and C the current position. The box obstructs passage.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q42.prompt: Which judgment matches the serving slip with the tray label?
options: P3 matches, so do not check different numbers.
Resident numbers differ; check before serving.
Independently change the right label to 012.
Put the tray down first if the seat is empty.
rationales: Matching texture P3 does not establish the correct recipient when numbers differ.
Serving slip 012 and tray 014 do not match, requiring a pre-serving check.
Changing the label independently alters identity without establishing the intended recipient.
An empty seat does not justify serving before identity matching.
kaigo-skills-mock-01-q42.figureDescription: The left serving slip shows resident 012, texture P3. The right tray label shows resident 014, texture P3.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q43.prompt: Before elimination support in the illustrated setting, what should be prioritized?
options: Leave entrance B open if care ends quickly.
Explain in corridor C and begin immediately.
Tell the person not to worry about corridor visibility.
Adjust and check visibility from the corridor.
rationales: Even brief corridor visibility fails to protect privacy.
Detailed corridor explanation and care can reveal private content or assistance to others.
Adjust surroundings instead of asking the person to disregard exposure.
This checks the open entrance and line of sight and provides necessary screening.
kaigo-skills-mock-01-q43.figureDescription: A is the elimination-support area, B the open entrance and C the corridor. The dotted line shows visibility from the corridor to A.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q44.prompt: Which response to the choice slip and prepared item is appropriate?
options: Treat the difference as color only and have the person wear S.
Treat prepared S as a changed personal choice.
Explain the R/S difference and check wishes again.
Rewrite R on the choice slip to match prepared S.
rationales: R and S differ in item code as well as color; they cannot be treated merely as color variants to wear.
Preparation differs from a personal change of choice.
Explain the difference between the choice slip and the prepared item, and check the person’s wishes.
Staff must not independently rewrite choices to match prepared items.
kaigo-skills-mock-01-q44.figureDescription: The left is the person’s choice slip for jacket R; the right shows prepared jacket S. R is blue and S green, but item codes as well as colors differ.

kaigo-skills-mock-01-q45.prompt: Under the illustrated sorting plan, what should happen to an untagged item?
options: Put untagged C into discard group B.
Put C into keep group A because it seems usable.
Swap A/B tags and choose the group closest to C.
Ask the person before sorting untagged C.
rationales: No tag does not mean disposal was permitted.
Staff judgment of usability alone does not decide personal storage.
Swapping personally assigned tags changes the chosen classification.
C’s handling is unconfirmed, so check with the person first.
kaigo-skills-mock-01-q45.figureDescription: The person designated blue-tagged items for storage in A and yellow-tagged items for disposal in B. C in the center has no tag.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q01.prompt: The person can address an envelope but finds small print difficult to see. Which supports independence?
options: Have family choose the recipient and the person copy it.
Make the information easier to read and let the person address it.
Write the entire address and letter because vision is difficult.
Do not adjust information because writing is possible.
rationales: This transfers recipient choice to family and removes personal decision-making.
This adjusts difficult-to-see information while preserving independent address writing.
Visual difficulty does not prove inability to write the address or letter. Check only necessary help.
Writing ability can coexist with a need for easier-to-read information.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q02.prompt: You want to use a resident’s photograph in training. What is appropriate?
options: Explain purpose and sharing scope, and check consent and facility procedures.
Skip checking with the person because the training is internal.
Treat consent to photography as consent to training use.
Removing names permits unrestricted sharing.
rationales: This clarifies the purpose and who will receive the information, and checks the person’s consent and the handling procedures.
Internal training does not remove the need to check purpose and sharing scope.
Photography consent does not necessarily include training use for another purpose.
Photographs may identify someone without names, so sharing is not unrestricted.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q03.prompt: Which profession specializes in swallowing training?
options: Registered dietitian.
Physical therapist.
Speech-language therapist.
Care manager.
rationales: Dietitians specialize in nutrition and meals; the swallowing-training profession asked here is the speech-language therapist.
Physical therapists address motor functions such as walking, distinct from the swallowing-training role asked here.
Speech-language therapists work with swallowing difficulties as well as language and hearing.
Care managers address plans and service coordination, not the swallowing-training specialty asked here.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q04.prompt: Which service involves staff visiting the person’s home for daily-life support?
options: Residential service.
Short-stay accommodation at a facility.
Home-visit service.
Day service.
rationales: Residential services support people living at a facility, not visits to their home.
Short stays involve accommodation at a facility, not staff visiting home.
Staff visiting the person’s home describes a home-visit service.
Day services involve the person attending a facility rather than a home visit.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q05.prompt: Which information belongs in a temperature record?
options: Measurement date/time, actual value and conditions.
Yesterday’s value entered as today’s.
Only a healthy-looking impression without values.
Only age and a guessed cause.
rationales: Date/time, actual value and conditions let recipients understand circumstances and changes.
Using yesterday’s value as today’s measurement makes the record inconsistent with facts.
A healthy-looking impression alone omits actual temperature and measurement conditions.
Age and guesses do not replace this measurement’s value, time and conditions.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q06.prompt: Which understanding of standard precautions is correct?
options: Gloves allow continued contact from dirty to clean areas.
Consider blood and excreta risks regardless of diagnosis.
Take care only with blood from diagnosed infections.
Clear body fluids can be handled bare-handed.
rationales: Gloves can be contaminated. Continued dirty-to-clean contact may spread it.
Standard precautions consider contact risks with blood, excreta and similar materials regardless of diagnosed infection.
People without a diagnosis can also carry infection; precautions are not diagnosis-limited.
Clear appearance does not establish absence of risk or permit bare-handed handling.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q07.prompt: Which workplace response reduces back strain?
options: Continue planned care unchanged despite back pain.
Lift alone regardless of weight if the task is familiar.
Check necessary staffing and equipment and avoid strenuous lifting.
Avoid fetching equipment and support with arm strength alone.
rationales: Pain calls for reviewing strain and methods and seeking advice rather than unchanged continuation.
Familiarity alone does not establish safe assistance conditions for the weight involved and the person’s condition.
Suitable equipment and staffing reduce workload and avoid excessive manual lifting.
Omitting equipment and relying on strength leaves safety conditions unmet for both people.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q08.prompt: Which principle supports adapting an entrance so wheelchair users can join community gatherings?
options: Keep the entrance unchanged and have them stop using aids.
Restrict disabled people to places separate from community activities.
Support community-living opportunities regardless of disability.
Treat family attendance as replacing personal participation.
rationales: Without environmental adjustments, removing equipment places the participation burden on the person alone.
Separation due to disability does not support opportunities in the same community.
This supports participation in community activities regardless of disability.
The family’s attendance does not replace the person’s participation or choice.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q09.prompt: While cleaning a room, you find a private letter. What is appropriate?
options: Photograph it for family contact without asking.
Do not read it; ask the person how to handle it.
Read it first to judge importance.
Discard old letters because tidying was requested.
rationales: A cleaning request does not establish consent to photography or family sharing.
This respects private content and checks wishes about the person’s property.
Judging importance does not justify reading private correspondence first.
Cleaning alone does not authorize discarding old letters without asking.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q10.prompt: A colleague requests a new assistance method you do not understand. What is appropriate?
options: Check the content and your role before starting.
Say you understand and guess during assistance.
Treat it as identical to a similar prior task.
Start with the resident and ask what steps mean afterward.
rationales: Checking unclear content and roles beforehand avoids acting by assumption.
Agreeing without understanding and guessing prevents shared methods and responsibilities.
Similar experience does not establish identical current people or conditions.
Check methods and roles before beginning rather than starting with uncertainties.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q11.prompt: Which pair forms the central nervous system?
options: Spinal cord and hand muscles.
Heart and autonomic nerves.
Brain and peripheral sensory nerves.
Brain and spinal cord.
rationales: The spinal cord is central; hand muscles are not central nervous structures.
The heart is a circulatory organ, so this pair does not describe the central nervous system.
The brain is central, but peripheral sensory nerves belong to the peripheral system.
The central nervous system consists of brain and spinal cord, distinguished from peripheral nerves.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q12.prompt: Which concept relates to sweating to regulate temperature in hot conditions?
options: Episodic memory.
Homeostasis.
Executive function.
Orientation.
rationales: Episodic memory concerns experiences, not temperature stabilization.
Homeostasis maintains bodily conditions within a range through responses such as sweating to environmental change.
Executive function includes planning and sequencing, distinct from this regulation concept.
Orientation concerns time/place awareness, distinct from homeostasis.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q13.prompt: Which part converts received sound vibrations into nerve signals?

Eardrum.
Cochlea.
Retina.

The eardrum receives sound as vibrations but differs from the converting cochlea.
The cochlea is the inner-ear part converting transmitted vibrations into nerve signals.
The retina concerns light in the eye, not ear vibrations.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q14.prompt: Which digestive-tract part mainly absorbs nutrients?

Esophagus.
Oral cavity.
Rectum.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q15.prompt: A person with dementia has difficulty organizing task sequences. Which impairment is related?

Hearing impairment.
Visual-field impairment.
Executive dysfunction.

Hearing impairment concerns hearing and is not established by sequencing difficulty alone.
Visual-field impairment concerns the visible area, not the planning function asked here.
Difficulty organizing and carrying out task steps relates to executive dysfunction.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q16.prompt: What matters when checking an older person’s condition?

Everyone of the same age has identical baselines.
Food intake alone establishes every physical and mental condition.
Compare with usual condition even without typical symptoms.
rationales: Symptoms can be atypical in older people; no fever alone does not rule out change.
Same-age people differ, so check the individual’s baseline.
Intake matters but cannot assess every physical and mental aspect alone.
Comparison with the person’s usual state can reveal change even when symptoms are subtle.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q17.prompt: The person says, ‘I felt tired in the crowded place today.’ Which reply shows active listening?

You dislike people. Let’s stop participation.
I know the reason; no more explanation is needed.
Next time should be fun, so don’t worry.
rationales: This acknowledges tiredness and asks about the setting.
This changes crowd-related fatigue into a personality judgment and cancellation.
This closes discussion before hearing reasons or feelings.
Predicting enjoyment next time does not adequately acknowledge current fatigue.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q18.prompt: What is appropriate when first addressing someone with limited sight?
options: Introduce yourself only to family, not the person.
Stand nearby silently until eye contact occurs.
Address the person and introduce your name and role.
Hold their hand first and ask them to guess who you are.
rationales: A person with limited sight still needs an explanation directly; introducing yourself only to the family does not replace it.
Silent waiting for eye contact does not tell someone with limited sight who is present.
Addressing and introducing yourself helps identify the speaker.
Touching before introduction and asking for a guess lacks advance notice and a check of wishes.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q19.prompt: Which record distinguishes the person’s own words from the worker’s observations?
options: Heavy-feeling legs establish heart disease.
The worker saw swelling, so the person also said it hurt.
The person stated ‘my legs feel heavy.’ The worker observed ankle swelling.
The person’s own words were excluded as mere impressions.
rationales: Heavy-feeling legs alone do not establish heart disease.
Observed swelling does not create a fact that pain was reported.
This separates the person’s statement and observed ankle condition by source.
The person’s own words help others understand their condition and should not be excluded from the record as mere impressions.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q20.prompt: You could not hear a time in the handover clearly. What is appropriate?
options: Identify the unclear time and check again.
Record it as yesterday’s time.
Omit the time check because other content was understood.
Infer a time from context and notify later.
rationales: Specifying the unclear point and asking again avoids retaining uncertain information.
Assuming yesterday’s time does not confirm this occasion.
Time matters for coordination. Understanding other details does not remove this uncertainty.
Check the correct time with the sender rather than deciding from context.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q21.prompt: Beyond walking to the dining room, what does mobility support contribute?
options: Arrival removes the need to check satisfaction.
Walking ability removes the need to ask about aids.
A familiar route needs no obstacle checks.
More opportunities for desired places and activities.
rationales: Arrival alone does not confirm the purpose was met or how the person feels.
Even someone able to walk needs checks of wishes and necessary equipment.
Objects and surfaces can change even on familiar routes. Check current conditions.
Mobility support expands access to desired places, activities and relationships.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q22.prompt: Which lying posture has the back down and face upward?
options: Supine.
Side-lying.
Sitting at the bed edge.
Prone.
rationales: Supine means lying on the back facing upward.
Side-lying places the body’s side down, unlike the stated back-down posture.
Bed-edge sitting has legs lowered and is not lying.
Prone places the front down, opposite to the description.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q23.prompt: You find new redness over the sacrum. What is appropriate?
options: Diagnose from color and apply medicine independently.
Rub the redness hard to improve circulation.
Omit records if the person reports no pain.
Report location and condition to healthcare professionals.
rationales: Color alone does not diagnose cause. Seek assessment rather than applying medicine on your own.
Hard rubbing does not replace pressure management or pressure-injury prevention.
Pain and redness are separate information. Record and report new redness even without pain.
Report the location and condition to healthcare professionals to support the necessary assessment and review of assistance.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q24.prompt: Which bedding conditions matter for pressure-injury risk?
options: Whether blanket colors match neighboring residents’.
Only washing date, without current inspection.
No wrinkle checks if the person chose the bedding.
Wrinkles against skin, moisture and bodily pressure.
rationales: Matching colors differs from checking pressure or bedding condition.
Washing date alone does not establish current wrinkles, moisture or pressure.
Personal choice does not remove checks of pressure-related wrinkles.
Skin-contact wrinkles, moisture and pressure are relevant risk checks.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q25.prompt: Which phase recognizes food by color and smell before it enters the mouth?
options: Pharyngeal.
Preparatory.
Anticipatory.
Esophageal.
rationales: The pharyngeal phase involves bolus passage through the pharynx, not pre-mouth recognition.
The preparatory phase chews food with saliva to form a bolus in the mouth.
Recognition by color, shape or smell before eating belongs to the anticipatory phase.
The esophageal phase moves food toward the stomach, not initial recognition.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q26.prompt: Food textures differ individually despite the same menu. What is appropriate when serving?
options: Give everyone the same food if it looks soft.
Ignore texture differences when dish names match.
Match individual meal instructions with the tray label.
Change texture among care staff alone if requested.
rationales: A soft appearance does not establish individual texture suitability or compliance with instructions.
Identical dishes may have different textures. Match labels and instructions.
Matching individual instructions and labels prevents inappropriate textures being served.
Wishes matter, but care staff do not independently change texture instructions.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q27.prompt: During a meal, the person says, ‘I would like a short rest.’ What is appropriate?
options: Pause eating and check condition and wishes.
Continue feeding because little remains.
Record the meal as finished because rest was requested.
Increase the amount without waiting for an answer.
rationales: Acknowledge the request, pause and check condition and subsequent wishes.
Little remaining food does not justify ignoring the wish or condition checks.
A temporary break differs from deciding to finish the meal.
Do not increase the amount without checking the person’s response; doing so omits necessary checks and disregards their wishes.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q28.prompt: The person holds a spoon but says a moving plate makes eating difficult. Which aid should be considered?
options: Oral foam swab.
Handled drinking cup.
Non-slip mat under the plate.
Large clothing button.
rationales: An oral swab serves oral cleanliness, not stabilizing a plate.
A handled cup helps drink handling, not directly the moving plate.
A non-slip mat can stabilize the plate while preserving spoon use.
A clothing button relates to dressing, not this dish movement.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q29.prompt: Which tube carries urine from the kidneys to the bladder?
options: Urethra.
Ureter.
Trachea.
Esophagus.
rationales: The urethra carries urine from the bladder outside, not kidneys to bladder.
Ureters carry urine produced in the kidneys to the bladder.
The trachea is an airway, not a urine pathway.
The esophagus transports swallowed material to the stomach, not urine.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q30.prompt: An unusual watery stool occurs. Which report is appropriate?
options: Record it as identical to someone else’s without looking.
Report the time, stool characteristics and what the person reports.
Report normal stool because yesterday was normal.
Conclude an infectious disease from one stool.
rationales: Another person’s stool or assumptions cannot be recorded as this person’s observation.
Specific timing, characteristics and complaints provide information to assess change.
Yesterday does not establish today’s condition. Report this observation.
One watery stool alone cannot establish an infectious-disease diagnosis.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q31.prompt: How should someone unable to find the toilet be supported?
options: Show the location clearly and check necessary mobility assistance.
Conclude they cannot sense the urge to urinate.
Make them wait until they memorize the location.
Decide one episode means permanent diaper use.
rationales: This clearly indicates location and checks help needed to reach it.
Location confusion does not establish absent urinary sensation.
Arrange support when elimination is needed rather than waiting for memorization.
One episode does not justify fixing all future care to diapers.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q32.prompt: After handling soiled items during a diaper change, what matters before touching clean supplies?
options: Prepare clean supplies with the same gloves.
Make appropriate glove and hand-hygiene transitions.
Check dirt only after touching clean items.
Treat glove removal as removing the need for hand hygiene.
rationales: Gloves used on dirty items can contaminate clean supplies.
Moving from dirty to clean tasks requires appropriate glove removal, hand hygiene and other necessary changes.
Make the transition before clean contact to avoid bringing contamination.
Hand hygiene is still needed after removal; gloves are not a complete substitute.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q33.prompt: What does grooming contribute to daily life?
options: Cleanliness removes the need to ask appearance preferences.
Changing clothes also completes health assessment.
Identical facility hairstyles remove personal choice.
It expresses preferences and individuality and supports relationships.
rationales: Grooming concerns preferences and appearance wishes as well as cleanliness.
Finished dressing does not establish completed health observation.
Uniform hairstyles do not respect individuality and choice.
Grooming helps express individuality and supports relationships.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q34.prompt: For a person with right-sided paralysis putting on a top, what is the general principle?
options: Insert the left arm first, then pull the right forcefully.
Preferred clothes remove the need to consider paralysis.
Insert the less mobile right arm first.
Always start on the same side when dressing and undressing.
rationales: Forcefully inserting the less mobile side afterward can increase strain and conflicts with the general principle.
Respect preferences while choosing methods that consider affected-side movement.

Generally dressing starts affected-side first and undressing unaffected-side first, not necessarily the same side.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q35.prompt: The skin around a nail is red and swollen. Which nail-care response is appropriate?

Cut deeply into swelling to remove the cause.
Cut as usual without checking because the person is hurried.
Report condition to healthcare professionals and confirm care methods.
rationales: Not yet having asked about pain does not establish that the observed redness or swelling is absent.
Care workers must not independently cut deeply into inflamed areas.
Urgency does not remove checks and consultation about a new abnormality.
Report nail or surrounding-skin abnormalities to healthcare professionals and check suitable care.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q36.prompt: What is a main purpose of oral hygiene regardless of teeth being present?
options: Without teeth, oral care has no purpose.
Maintain cleanliness and reduce oral bacteria.
No meals means no oral-cleanliness checks.
Toothbrushing establishes normal swallowing.
rationales: Oral cleanliness still matters without teeth; care remains meaningful.
Cleanliness and bacterial reduction matter whether teeth remain or not.
Not eating does not remove oral-hygiene checks.
Toothbrushing alone does not assess swallowing as normal.

options: Use only boiling water for every denture.
Replace without cleaning whenever dirt is invisible.
Mix them with another person’s and identify by shape.
Verify ownership and clean according to material and procedures.
rationales: Do not use boiling water uniformly. Check product instructions and suitable methods.
No visible dirt does not establish that cleaning is unnecessary; maintain appropriate hygiene.
Do not mix different people’s dentures; prevent identification errors.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q38.prompt: Why check room temperature before bathing?

To reduce abrupt temperature differences between changing and bathing rooms.
A suitable room temperature removes the need to check the person’s condition.
Yesterday’s reading removes today’s checks.
rationales: Room and water temperatures are separate; measuring one does not establish the other.
Check the environment so that there is no abrupt temperature difference between the changing room and the bathroom.
Checking room temperature does not replace checking the person’s condition before bathing.
Temperatures can change, so yesterday alone does not confirm today’s environment.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q39.prompt: During a bed bath, how should areas not yet being wiped be treated?
options: Expose only necessary areas and cover the others.
No covering is needed if the person cannot see.
Expose the whole body from the start for speed.
Consent removes checks of covering arrangements.
rationales: Limited exposure and covering protect privacy and warmth.
Whether the person can see the exposed area does not by itself remove the need to limit exposure.
Treat necessary areas in sequence rather than exposing everything for speed.
Consent does not remove consideration of exposure scope or covering.

kaigo-skills-mock-02-q40.prompt: When clearing items from the floor, what supports the person’s life?

Check safety and wishes and discuss storage locations.
Move items daily for a uniform appearance.
Do nothing about fall risks because items belong to the person.
rationales: Safety does not mean discarding every possession.
This checks fall hazards and discusses placement according to wishes.
Daily staff-preference rearrangements can impair familiar routines and usability.
Respect ownership while discussing and addressing safety together.

Check only water temperature and the step after use.
Check floor water and the step and arrange a safe environment.

Bathing wishes and environmental safety are separate requirements.

This checks wet area A and step B before use and arranges safety.

kaigo-skills-mock-03-q01.prompt: The person declines an activity. After hearing why, what is appropriate?

Cancel every support task that day.

Quiet speech removes consent and sharing-scope checks.

Record no change because of age.

One worker’s use makes classification unnecessary.
Gloves remove dirt from equipment.
To avoid carrying contamination to clean areas or other people.

The same user does not prevent equipment-mediated contamination.
Gloves do not clean the equipment and may themselves spread contamination.
Separate used and clean items to avoid bringing contamination elsewhere.

Leave every duty with colleagues without checking their assignments.
Do not report because the worker looks normal to residents.

Normal appearance differs from experienced severe fatigue and does not justify withholding a report.

kaigo-skills-mock-03-q08.prompt: Why avoid language or names that treat a resident as a child?
options: Changing address alone secures every consent.
To respect adult dignity and preferred forms of address.
To use one identical name for everyone older.
Familiarity removes the need to ask preferences.
rationales: Respectful address matters but does not complete other explanations or consent.
Respect the person as an adult and check how they wish to be addressed.

Feeling familiar does not permit guessing someone’s preference.

Postpone contact until the cause field is filled.
Report confirmed events and the unconfirmed cause separately.
rationales: Presenting a guessed cause as fact mixes observations with judgments for later assessment.

kaigo-skills-mock-03-q10.prompt: The person and family disagree about daily-life plans. What should a care worker do?

Stop all explanations and consultations because opinions differ.
Decide by staff convenience without hearing either side.

Record every anxiety report as memory impairment.
Use identical words for everyone with the same diagnosis.

kaigo-skills-mock-03-q17.prompt: A worker repeatedly changes topics before the person finishes. What improves the exchange?

kaigo-skills-mock-03-q23.prompt: Which understanding of reduced strength and joint movement after prolonged inactivity is appropriate?

Increase identical exercise for everyone without checks.
rationales: Prolonged low activity-related muscle and joint changes should be considered in a planned response to disuse.
